translation:
For a man to have eyes is like heaven having the sun and moon. If heaven had no sun and moon, by what would one distinguish yin and yang? If a man had no eyes, by what would he distinguish the colors of things?

Therefore the eye is the organ that governs seeing, and the five channels of the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys are all attached to it. Then how could the eye fail to be bright? Alas, those in the world who suffer from eye disease are many. Some, through wine and lust, give rise to star-shaped opacities; some, through wind and fire, produce cloud-like films. Without good medicine, how could they be treated? Yet good medicine cannot be used unless there is a good physician. I once heard Master Su say, "Though the medicine is administered by the physician's hand, the formulas are mostly transmitted from the ancients." Truly these words are excellent. Now those who make their living by the three-finger pulse diagnosis, without considering the meaning that "the physician works by intention," and without investigating the source of the disease, recklessly administer medicines and thereby cause lifelong blindness. This is truly lamentable. I reflect that in a town of ten households there must be loyal and trustworthy men, and the world is vast—how could there be a lack of good physicians? If one who can restore the blind to sight makes them wander again beneath the bright sky and open sun, how great is his merit! Governor Hu Zhijiao, a renowned scholar of Guichuan, once served in the Wu and Chu regions with many benevolent policies. When he was transferred to be magistrate of Shaxian and Longxi in Min, he deeply mastered the art of leniency and severity of Guo Qiao, the people were harmonious, and wherever he went they sang his praises, missing him when he left and rejoicing at his coming. I have shared a boat with him for ten years, and I knew only that the Governor's learning was profound and deep, that he devoted himself to antiquity, and that the writings stored in his belly were surely more than five thousand scrolls. I never knew that he was versed in the learning of Qi and Huang. Only because his family members, when occasionally ill, never summoned a physician from outside, did I secretly wonder. Last winter my wife suffered from wheezing and was near death several times. Someone said the Governor could cure her, so I invited him to my residence. He administered a dose, and in the end she was saved by it. Is the Governor not the reincarnation of Bian Que? On that occasion he showed me a hand-copied ophthalmology text published by Nian Ouzhai, a book by Master Deng of Qingjiang, to which was appended a transmission of the Seventy-Two Questions and Answers on Ophthalmology, combined into one volume, re-collated, and named The True Meaning of Enlightenment. He had kept it for years, and not wishing to keep it secret and boast of its marvels, he hastened to put it into print to share it with those of like mind. He then asked me for a preface. I am ashamed of my own shallowness and ignorance of medical principles—how dare I write a preface to this book? Alas, this is truly asking the way of a blind man. Now I see that this book is orderly and not confused, complete in meaning and principle, and its application is so divine that it cannot be fathomed with a gourd ladle. It is truly a book never before seen in ophthalmology. How fortunate am I to see it! Now, upon unrolling the scroll, I understand it clearly within myself, and I say that it will enlighten not only my own ignorance but the ignorance of millions in the world. That the Governor named this book The True Meaning of Enlightenment—who can say it is not so?

<ins>Respectfully written by Cao Jinchi of Jiashan at the House of the Inchworm, west of Green Banyan City, on the day after the Lantern Festival in the renwu year of the Guangxu reign</ins>
translator_notes: 三指禅 (three-finger meditation) refers to pulse diagnosis, hence the medical profession.
國僑 (Guo Qiao) refers to Zichan of Zheng.
蠡測 (measuring with a gourd) means fathoming something deep with a shallow vessel.
鉛槧 (lead and wooden slips) refers to printing.
